questions.topic: Y-intercept of a factored quadratic
questions.learningObjective: explain how a y-intercept is read from a factored rule
questions.stem: The glossary has to explain how a y-intercept is read from a factored rule, with a short worked example.

answer.exemplar: The y-intercept is the output of a rule when the input is zero, so a factored rule only has to be read at x equal to 0. For y = (x - 2)(x + 5) that gives the product -2 times 5, which is -10, and this is why a factored rule is often used to read an intercept quickly. The trap is to add the bracket constants, which for this rule would give 3 and describe no point on the rule at all. Another trap is to assume that a factored rule passes through the origin, which happens only when one of the brackets is simply x.

questions.explanation: The y-intercept is the output at input zero, and a factored rule gives that as a product of the bracket values. Adding them instead produces a number that no point of the rule has.
questions.hint: The intercept is a product of the bracket values.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Linear coefficient after expanding a vertex form
questions.learningObjective: explain how a linear coefficient arises from a vertex form
questions.stem: The glossary should work through one example to show how the linear coefficient arises from a vertex form.

answer.exemplar: A rule written with a square hides its linear term, and expanding the square reveals it. For y = (x - 3)^2 + 4 the square gives x^2 - 6x + 9, so the finished rule is x^2 - 6x + 13 and the linear coefficient is -6. The pattern is that the number inside the bracket is doubled and its sign reversed, because a negative shift is multiplied by -1 twice in the expansion. The constant 4 outside the square never touches the x term, which is why a rule can be raised or lowered without changing where it turns.

questions.explanation: Expanding the square produces the linear term, because the cross terms multiply the bracket value by the input and add it to itself. The outside constant changes only the constant, so it never touches the linear coefficient.
questions.hint: The bracket number is doubled and its sign flipped.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Smallest value on a restricted interval
questions.learningObjective: explain why an endpoint can be the smallest value on an interval
questions.stem: The glossary must explain why a restricted interval sometimes makes an endpoint the smallest value.

answer.exemplar: A rule that opens upward has one lowest point, and that point is reached wherever the input is allowed to be. When the interval contains the turning point, the smallest value is the value of the turn, and the endpoints can only be larger. When the interval stops short of the turn, the rule is still falling at the near edge, so the smallest value is the one at the endpoint closest to the turn. For y = x^2 - 6x + 5 on the interval from 0 to 2, the turn at x = 3 is out of reach, so the value 5 falls to -3 and the smallest is -3. A glossary that quotes the vertex value without looking at the interval is describing a point the reader cannot reach.

questions.explanation: The smallest value on an interval is the least of the turning point and the two endpoints. When the turn is out of reach the nearest endpoint takes its place, and quoting the vertex alone ignores the interval.
questions.hint: Compare the turning point with the interval's edges.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Axis read from the roots of a factored rule
questions.learningObjective: explain why the axis lies halfway between the roots
questions.stem: The glossary should explain the symmetry that puts the axis of a factored rule halfway between its roots.

answer.exemplar: A rule with two roots has zeros at those inputs, and the shape of a quadratic is symmetric, so the picture on one side of the midpoint must match the picture on the other. For y = (x - 2)(x - 6) the two crossings are 2 and 6, and the axis of symmetry is the midpoint, 4. Checking confirms it, because the rule gives -8 at x = 3 and at x = 5, the same distance from 4. Adding the roots instead of averaging them gives 8, which is twice the axis, a slip that is easy to make when the two roots have the same sign.

questions.explanation: A quadratic is symmetric about one vertical line, and the two roots sit on either side of that line at equal distances. Adding the roots gives twice the axis, which is why halving the sum is the step that is often missed.
questions.hint: Symmetry means the midpoint of the crossings.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Greatest profit from a quadratic model
questions.learningObjective: explain how the greatest profit is read from a quadratic model
questions.stem: The glossary should explain, with numbers, how the greatest profit is read from a quadratic model.

answer.exemplar: A profit model that opens downward, such as P = -2x^2 + 16x - 20, is highest at one selling point, and that point is the vertex, whose input is -b over 2a. Here that is -16 over -4, which is 4 units, and the profit at 4 units is -32 plus 64 minus 20, which is 12. Reading the constant 20 as the profit would describe selling nothing, and reading the linear coefficient 16 as the profit would describe no situation at all. The glossary should also warn that the model only holds over the range of quantities the business can actually sell.

questions.explanation: The greatest profit of a downward model is the value at the vertex, and the vertex input is -b over 2a. A coefficient is not a profit, and the constant is only the profit at zero units.
questions.hint: The peak of a downward model is its best selling point.

questions.topic: Length of a rectangle found from an area condition
questions.learningObjective: explain how an area condition produces the sides of a rectangle
questions.stem: The glossary should work through how an area condition produces the sides of a rectangle, with one example.

answer.exemplar: When a rectangle has a width of x and a length of 12 - x, the area is the product x(12 - x), and setting that product to a stated area gives a quadratic. For an area of 35 square units the equation is x^2 - 12x + 35 equals zero, whose roots are 5 and 7, so the rectangle is 5 by 7 and the area checks out at 35. The two roots are not two different rectangles, they are the same rectangle described from opposite sides. A reader who reports the area as a side length, or who halves the total instead of solving, will usually get a number that does not multiply back to the stated area.

questions.explanation: The area of a rectangle is the product of its sides, so a stated area turns into a quadratic in the width. The two roots are the same rectangle read from opposite sides, and each must multiply back to the stated area.
questions.hint: The area is a product of the two sides.

questions.topic: Nonzero solution of an equation with a zero constant term
questions.learningObjective: explain why a zero constant term leaves the input 0 as a solution
questions.stem: The glossary should explain the reason a zero constant term always leaves the input 0 as one solution.

answer.exemplar: An equation such as x^2 - 5x equals 0 can be written as the product x(x - 5) equals zero, because a zero constant term means the product has an x in it. A product is zero exactly when one of its factors is zero, so the input 0 always satisfies the equation, whatever else the rule looks like. The other solution comes from the remaining factor, and here it is 5, so the two solutions are 0 and 5. Students who divide through by x lose the zero input, which is why factoring is the safer first move when the constant term is zero.

questions.explanation: A zero constant term lets the rule be factored by x, and a product is zero when either factor is zero, so the input 0 is always a solution. Dividing by x first would lose it.
questions.hint: A zero constant means the rule can be factored by x.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Positive solution of a quadratic with a non-square discriminant
questions.learningObjective: explain why a non-square discriminant needs an exact or rounded answer
questions.stem: The glossary should explain why the discriminant of a quadratic decides the form of its answers.

answer.exemplar: The discriminant decides what kind of answer a quadratic can give. When it is a perfect square, the formula produces a fraction with no remainder and the solution is a neat number, but when the discriminant is 21 the square root of 21 cannot be simplified, so the solution is irrational and has no exact decimal form. For x^2 + x - 5 equals 0 the positive solution is (-1 + the square root of 21) over 2, which is about 1.79. A glossary should ask for the exact form when the numbers are awkward and a rounded value when the answer is meant for measurement, and should say which one it is using.

questions.explanation: A non-square discriminant leaves a square root that cannot be simplified, so the solution has no exact decimal form. The glossary should say whether it wants the exact expression or a rounded value.
questions.hint: An irrational root has no exact decimal value.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Evaluating a quadratic at a negative input
questions.learningObjective: explain how a negative input behaves in a quadratic rule
questions.stem: The glossary should walk through a negative input to show how the signs behave in a quadratic rule.

answer.exemplar: A negative input changes two of the three terms of a quadratic rule in different ways, and both changes have to be carried through. For y = x^2 - 7x + 4 at x equal to -2, the squared term is 4 because a square is never negative, the linear term is -7 times -2, which is 14 because two negatives make a positive, and the constant is untouched, so the value is 22. The slip that appears most often in glossaries is treating the negative input as positive in the linear term, which would give -6, and readers who only square the input forget that the sign still matters one term further along.

questions.explanation: A square always removes the sign of the input, while the linear term keeps it and can flip it again. Both behaviours have to be carried through term by term.
questions.hint: A square loses the sign, but the linear term does not.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Time at which a downward model returns to zero
questions.learningObjective: explain how a landing time is found from a downward model
questions.stem: The glossary should explain how a landing time is found from a downward model, with a worked example.

answer.exemplar: A downward model that starts above the ground comes back down to it, and the time of that return is found by setting the model equal to zero and keeping the later root. For h = -2t^2 + 12t - 10, the equation 2t^2 - 12t + 10 equals zero divides by 2 to t^2 - 6t + 5 equals zero, which factors to (t - 1)(t - 5), so the model touches the ground at 1 second and again at 5 seconds. The peak of the model, at 3 seconds in this case, tells only when the height is greatest, and a glossary that reports the peak as a landing time will confuse the two ideas.

questions.explanation: The landing times are the roots of the equation that sets the model equal to zero, and the later root is the return. The peak of the model is a different idea and must not be reported as a landing time.
questions.hint: Set the model to zero and keep the later root.
